description: We’re nasawat, three friends from Algiers: Abderraouf, Mohamed Reda and Mohamed Achraf. We’re computer science students who love space and building in practice not theory. This was our first time digging into real NASA experiment data, and honestly it was messy, but that’s what made it fun. Hope Fotia you enjoy our project
summary:
Fotia is a web dashboard that predicts how a droplet of fuel burns in a spacecraft’s air, and tells you how close each answer is to a real NASA test. NASA’s microgravity combustion results are public on the Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) repository, but they sit in 24 investigations with no common format. We read all 24, sorted them in the app by what their data can answer, and trained models on 236 droplet burns from the ISS FLEX experiment and Spacelab MSL-1. 

A visitor picks a real spacecraft atmosphere (ISS, Orion, Soyuz, NASA’s proposed exploration atmosphere) or their own mix, watches a 3D flame burn at the computed rate, and learns whether it goes out, how fast it burns and how long it lasts. Every answer carries a badge, Measured here, Between tests or Never tested, because NASA’s tests cover little of the space: on FLEX only 31 of 196 oxygen–CO₂ combinations were tested. This matters for lunar habitats, whose richer, thinner air lies partly outside every test, and it shows NASA where to test next.
details:
What it does

Fotia predicts how a droplet of fuel burns in a spacecraft’s air, and tells you how close each answer is to a real NASA test. The page reads top to bottom in six steps:
01 Where: pick one of seven real spacecraft atmospheres (ISS cabin air, ISS airlock and Shuttle before a spacewalk, Orion’s lunar design and full-pressure atmospheres, Soyuz, NASA’s proposed exploration atmosphere), each with a cited source, or your own mix.
02 The air: sliders for oxygen, pressure, gravity and droplet size; fuel (methanol, heptane, n-decane); diluent (nitrogen, CO₂, helium). A green band under each slider shows the range NASA tested; beyond it the value turns red.
03 The flame: a 3D WebGL flame that shrinks at the computed rate, with the diameter curve over time.
04 Prediction: whether the flame goes out (and at what diameter, with its probability), the burning rate constant K and its ratio to ISS air, the burn time, and a confidence badge.
05 Why it matters: a map of real spacecraft atmospheres with NASA-STD-3001 crew limits and your setting on it, then real fires and published results that match it, each quoted and linked.
06 The data: all 24 NASA PSI combustion investigations in one table, with NASA’s own title, where and when each flew, how many clean rows came out (1,244 in all), and our reading of each. 7 are fully used, 3 partly usable and 14 hold no per-test outcome.

A floating SI assistant, Ask Fotia, answers questions about the dashboard and the science.

How it works

Burning rate: ridge regression on 236 burns (204 FLEX droplets on the ISS, PSI-69, plus 32 heptane droplets from Spacelab MSL-1, NASA/TM-2003-212553). Cross-validated R² 0.64, typical error 0.05 mm²/s. A 300-tree random forest did worse (R² 0.61).

Extinction: logistic regression with balanced class weights on 206 FLEX burns. 87% of them went out, so “always extinguishes” scores 87% and finds none of the full burns. Fotia reaches a balanced accuracy of 0.75 and a ROC AUC of 0.83, and finds 78% of the burns that went to completion. Extinction diameter: ridge regression, R² 0.75.

Droplet life follows the d² law (d² = d₀² − K·t), checked against 158 measured burns: correlation 0.995, median error 6%.

Beyond the tested range, K comes from the learned value at the edge times the ln(1+B) ratio of Spalding’s droplet theory. That theory underestimates the oxygen effect by about 20–25% on FLEX, and the app says so. Extinction is never extrapolated.

Ask Fotia runs on Google Gemini but cannot compute a number itself. Through function calling it uses five tools (current setting, predict, list places, tested ranges, search sources) and quotes what comes back, with the badge. It refuses anything outside spacecraft fire safety.

How it is creative: the confidence badge

Every answer carries one of three badges: Measured here, Between tests or Never tested. The threshold is not hand-picked: Fotia measures how far each real test sits from its nearest neighbour, and that distribution defines a normal neighbourhood. This matters because two values tested separately do not make a tested combination. On FLEX, only 31 of the 196 oxygen × CO₂ combinations were ever tested; a slider grid of 6,400 positions hits only 40 tested cells (99.4% untested). Fotia shows this honestly instead of giving the same confident number everywhere.

Benefits and intended impact

  • Spacecraft fire-safety engineers and cabin designers get a first-pass check of a new atmosphere. Orion’s 10.2 psi, 30% O₂ lunar design is “Measured here”, but NASA’s proposed 8.2 psi, 34% exploration atmosphere is “Never tested”: the low-pressure end of the planned Moon-base air lies outside every droplet test in the data.
  • Researchers and NASA planners can see where NASA has not tested, and so where the next ISS combustion experiment would teach the most.
  • Students and the public see why flames are spheres in space and why oxygen and pressure matter (Apollo 1).

It is free and open source, and runs in a browser. Each new NASA experiment added to the data turns more of the map green.

Factors we considered

  • Small data (hundreds of rows), so we used classical ML by design: models chosen by cross-validation, coefficients checked against physics, and features known before ignition kept apart from post-burn measurements to prevent leakage.
    • Every droplet test is in microgravity, and PSI holds no partial-gravity combustion data yet, so above microgravity only the drawn shape changes.
    • n-decane is computed from heptane and labelled so.
    • Flame colour and flicker are illustrative; sizes and times are computed.
    • Some context quotes are not yet verified against their originals, and the app labels them.

Tools

Python (pandas, NumPy, scikit-learn, Streamlit, google-genai), JavaScript, HTML and CSS for the console, WebGL2 and GLSL for the raymarched flame, Google Gemini API, deployed on Streamlit Community Cloud, code on GitHub.
